Instructions

In this lab you will compare movements of the hindlimb during the bipedal walking of three individuals. You will use this motion analysis software to collect data on the position of the hip as well as the degree of flexion and extension of the knee and thigh. Through this analysis, you will be able to comment on important differences between both human and non-human primate bipedalism as well as differences between adult and juvenile human bipedalism.

During the instructions section, you can navigate through the screens using the buttons located in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. When you reach the end of the instructions section, you will be directed to the first data collection section of this lab.

Kinematics Methods

Kinematics is the quantitative study of motion. In order to perform a kinematics analysis you must first film subjects walking or running. After the subjects have been filmed, the video must be captured onto the computer so that clips can be analyzed frame-by-frame. Once captured, the video must be loaded into a kinematics software package (such as the one you are using now) and then you are ready to collect data. You will begin with a video clip of an adult human walking bipedally on a treadmill. You will be able to advance frame-by-frame through the clip. Before starting the lab, play the clip below a couple of times to get an overall sense of hindlimb motion. Learn how the controller below the clip works by clicking on each button. Also notice that each frame is numbered in the top right-hand corner of the screen.

Collecting Data

Notice that a green dot appears where you clicked. This dot will help you identify whether or not you clicked on the correct joint. When you do the lab exercise, you will be directed to identify the knee and ankle joints as well. As you collect these data, their coordinates will appear in the boxes in the lower left-hand corner of the screen. Now press Next.

Hindlimb Joint Angles

After you have collected your kinematics data, you must analyze the variable of interest. In this lab, you will be examining three variables: knee flexion and extension during bipedalism, hip flexion and extension, and the position of the hip at different points throughout the stride. The three subjects will all have different kinematics even though they use the same form of locomotion (bipedalism). In order to understand what happens to these different joints throughout locomotion, you will plot each variable as a function of time. Below is an example of a plot of knee flexion angle as a function of time. Click on the blue terms to learn how to interpret this graph.

Interpreting the Thigh Angle

In addition to the knee angle, you will analyze the orientation of the thigh during bipedalism in the three subjects. This orientation is measured as the angle of the thigh with respect to a vertical axis perpendicular to the ground. So, the thigh is flexed when the angle is low and extended when the angle is high. Again, click on the blue terms to learn how to interpret the plot below.

Interpreting the Hip Position

Finally, you will examine how the position of the hip changes throughout the stride. The data below show how far the hip is above or below its average height, as a percentage of limb length (the distance from the hip to the ankle). You will decide at what points in the stride the hip is at its highest and lowest.

Finding the Step Events

When you have finished collecting the kinematics data, you will need to find the step events for each video clip. To do this, you will click the “Step Events” button next to the movie controls. Once you click this button, the step events recorder window appears in the upper right-hand portion of the screen. Using the movie controls, you will find the frame when touchdown occurs and then click the “Touchdown” button. You will do this for the other three step events and then click the “Done” button. If you want to practice finding step events, click the step events button now. Otherwise, click “Next” to begin the lab.

Begin the Lab
